facts.title: Born From a Rainbow
facts.text: Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by German scientists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, the pioneers of flame spectroscopy. They spotted two brilliant deep-red spectral lines in mineral water from Bad Dürkheim that matched no known element. The name comes from the Latin 'rubidus', meaning 'deepest red', after those signature lines.

facts.title: Melts in Your Hand (Almost)
facts.text: Rubidium is so soft and low-melting that it would turn liquid at about 39.3 degrees Celsius (102.7 F), just a few degrees above body temperature. It is a silvery metal soft enough to cut with a knife. Because of this, it is one of only a handful of metals that can be molten on a warm summer day.

facts.title: Violently Allergic to Water
facts.text: As an alkali metal, rubidium reacts explosively with water, producing hydrogen gas and enough heat to ignite it instantly. It also bursts into flame on contact with air, so it must be stored under dry mineral oil or in sealed glass ampoules under inert gas. This extreme reactivity is why pure rubidium is never found free in nature.

facts.title: Hiding in Plain Sight
facts.text: Rubidium is actually the 23rd most abundant element in Earth's crust, more common than copper or zinc. Yet it has no ores of its own and is always scattered as a minor companion inside potassium minerals like lepidolite, pollucite, and carnallite. Most commercial rubidium is recovered as a byproduct of refining lithium and cesium.

facts.title: A Built-In Atomic Clock
facts.text: About 28 percent of natural rubidium is the radioactive isotope rubidium-87, which decays into strontium-87 with a half-life of roughly 49 billion years, far longer than the age of the universe. Geologists exploit this rubidium-strontium decay to date rocks and meteorites that are billions of years old. The same isotope made rubidium a key tool in measuring the age of the Solar System.

facts.title: Heart of the Atomic Clock
facts.text: Rubidium is the working element in compact, affordable atomic clocks used to keep time with extraordinary precision. Rubidium clocks ride aboard GPS satellites and anchor cellular networks, drifting by only a fraction of a second over thousands of years. Their small size and low cost make them the workhorse atomic clock of modern telecommunications.

facts.title: The Coldest Stuff Ever Made
facts.text: In 1995, physicists Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman used a cloud of about 2,000 rubidium-87 atoms to create the first Bose-Einstein condensate, a bizarre state of matter predicted by Einstein 70 years earlier. They cooled the atoms to within billionths of a degree of absolute zero, the coldest temperatures ever achieved. This breakthrough earned a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics.

facts.title: Cousin to Potassium
facts.text: Because rubidium ions behave chemically much like potassium, your body actually absorbs small amounts of it from food, and an average adult carries roughly half a gram of it. It is not a required nutrient and has no known biological function, but the body treats it as a harmless potassium stand-in. Concentrations are highest in muscle tissue.

facts.title: Tracing the Beating Heart
facts.text: Doctors use radioactive rubidium-82 as a tracer in PET scans to image blood flow through the heart muscle. Injected into a vein, it follows the same paths as potassium and lights up healthy versus damaged heart tissue. With a half-life of just 75 seconds, it delivers its picture and then vanishes almost immediately, keeping radiation exposure very low.

facts.title: Painting the Flame Purple
facts.text: When rubidium compounds are heated in a flame, they glow a striking reddish-violet, a direct visual echo of the red spectral lines that revealed the element. This property is sometimes used in specialty fireworks and signal flares to produce purple hues. The same effect lets chemists identify rubidium with a simple flame test.
